summary: Extends the Protocol Identifier Reference for the Remote Network Monitoring MIB, version 2, with ways to identify protocol operations, called verbs, inside the protocols being monitored. It does not obsolete the earlier reference and it updates RFC 2895.

eli5.summary: A traffic counter can tell which road a car is on. These extra rules let it also tell what the car is doing, for example which request an application is making.

subtitle: A way to name individual application operations, such as an FTP command, inside RMON protocol identifiers.

tldr.problem: RMON could identify which protocol a packet belongs to, but not which operation within an application protocol it performs, even though operations can perform very differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a VERB-IDENTIFIER macro that maps verb names to integers, and an extra 4-octet verb layer appended to the parent application's protocol identifier.
tldr.outcome: Probes can count traffic per application operation. The RFC updates RFC 2895 without obsoleting any part of it, and defines no new MIB objects.

today: RFC 3395 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2895 and obsoletes nothing. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Overview and Relationship to RMON
sections.content:
Different operations of an application protocol can have very different performance, so it is useful to collect metrics at that level. This memo extends the RMON protocol identifier structure of RFC 2895 to cover application verbs. It updates that document and does not obsolete any portion of it.

In the existing structure each layer adds 4 octets to the protocolDirID string and one octet to the protocolDirParameters string. Together these two objects index the protocolDirTable of RFC 2021 (RMON-2). A verb is simply one more layer appended to its parent application.

The memo defines no new MIB objects and no MIB module. Other specifications that use the RMON-2 protocol directory can use the same verb macros.
sections.eli5: RMON already has a naming scheme for kinds of traffic. This adds one more step to the name so you can say not just what program, but what job the program is doing.

sections.title: Verbs and Related Terms
sections.content:
An application verb is one of the protocol operations an application protocol defines. It is not the same as a single opcode or PDU type: a verb is a transaction type and may involve several PDU types, such as an SNMP Get-PDU and its Response-PDU. A verb may even span more than one protocol directory entry, such as ftp and ftp-data.

The connect verb covers connection or session setup and tear-down traffic not attributed to any other verb. It has the value zero, and connect(0) is implicitly defined for every application protocol.

The parent application is the protocol encapsulation that identifies the application. The verb layer is the part of the identifier that names the verb, and a verb set is the group of verbs enumerated for one protocol.
sections.eli5: A verb is one kind of job, like asking to download a file. Setting up and hanging up the call is a special job called connect, which always has the number zero.

sections.title: The Verb Identifier Macro
sections.content:
The PI language gains one keyword, VERB-IDENTIFIER. A definition names the parent protocol, gives a required DESCRIPTION, an optional REFERENCE, and a list of verbs, each written as a lowercase name with a number such as user(1).

The parent protocol name SHOULD be an ASCII string of 1 to 64 characters and MUST name a protocol defined in the same file. The REFERENCE clause SHOULD be present when an authoritative document defines the verbs.

At least one verb MUST be listed, and up to 16,777,215 MAY be. Numbers SHOULD be dense, from 1 to N. Verb names are case-sensitive, MUST be unique within a parent application, and SHOULD follow the authoritative document's own names. Each number MUST be unique too. The number zero MUST NOT be redefined, though the name connect may be reused for another number.
sections.eli5: It is a form where you list each job an application can do and give each one its own number, with no repeats.

sections.title: Protocol Directory Mapping
sections.content:
The verb layer is 4 octets in the protocolDirID. The first octet is reserved and MUST be zero. The next three hold the verb number as a 24-bit unsigned integer in network byte order. A verb ID is written [0.a.b.c], from 0.0.0.0 (the implicit connect verb) up to 0.255.255.255. The full protocolDirID is the parent's ID followed by these four octets.

The protocolDirParameters value is the parent's value plus one octet of zero, kept only to follow the RFC 2895 encoding rules.

An agent MUST implement all applicable protocolDirTable objects for each verb. It conveys the verb name in protocolDirDescr, which SHOULD be the parent's description, a dot, then the verb name. It MUST set protocolDirType to the empty bit set and protocolDirAddressMapConfig to notSupported(1). Host and matrix configuration depend on what the agent can monitor per verb, and MAY follow the parent's setting.
sections.eli5: The verb's address is the program's address with a short extra number stuck on the end. The first part of that extra number is always zero, and the rest says which job.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Counting at the verb layer often needs state. An SNMP Response-PDU to a Get looks the same as one to a Getnext, so a probe must remember the request. For stream protocols such as TCP, a verb can span several packets, so the probe must follow the flow.

Packet capture filtered by verb may need to wait until a packet can be attributed to a verb, so a probe may have to pre-buffer packets.

RMON-2 collections count each packet once, as a single leaf entry in the protocol directory, and add the whole packet size to octet counters. If a packet holds several verb types, the agent MUST pick one. How is implementation specific; options include the first verb seen, the most frequent, the one using the most octets, or the most interesting.
sections.eli5: To know what job a message belongs to, the counter sometimes has to remember earlier messages. If one message has several jobs in it, the counter picks one to count it under.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
The appendix defines verb sets for five protocols: FTP (42 commands such as user(1) and retr(14)), POP3 (13 commands), SNMP, HTTP and SMTP.

The SNMP set lists transaction types, and treats Response and Report PDUs as part of the transaction of the request, not as verbs. The SMTP set adds an xcmd verb as a catch-all for private-use commands starting with X. The HTTP set shows an explicit connect(8), reserved for future use, alongside the implicit connect(0).
sections.eli5: The examples show filled-in forms for file transfer, mail, web and network management, each listing its own jobs and numbers.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The memo defines no MIB objects or protocol operations, only how to represent verbs in RMON protocol identifiers, and the RFC says it introduces no new security risks. However, a collection built on these identifiers may reveal which verbs of an application protocol are used on a network, which may need extra protection. MIB writers should address that.

No verbs are defined that need IANA registration. The RFC notes it is remotely possible that a future version will define some in the ianaAssigned subtree.
sections.eli5: Counting which jobs people do could tell nosy people what is going on, so whoever builds a counter should think about who can see the results.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use; MUST be set to zero.

fields.name: Verb enumeration value
fields.desc: The verbEnum, as a 24-bit unsigned integer in network byte order.
